sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces early distress in concrete pavements, occurring while concrete is plastic or soon after hardening. Identifying the cause and applying corrective measures is essential to reduce recurrence; disposition of distressed slabs should be discussed at pre-construction meetings. Lists the four commonly encountered early distress types covered in this chapter.
sections.body: Concrete pavements can exhibit early distress. This occurs while the concrete is in a plastic state or soon after hardening. When early distress is observed, the cause of the failure must be identified and appropriate corrective measures taken to reduce the potential for reoccurrence. It is good practice to discuss the disposition of slabs that exhibit early distress at the pre-construction meetings, so that the project team has an agreed-upon protocol before problems arise in the field. The commonly encountered early distress types addressed in this chapter are plastic shrinkage cracking, edge slump, joint spalling, and full-depth cracking.
key_points: Early distress occurs while concrete is plastic or soon after hardening.
Identify the cause of any early distress and apply corrective measures to prevent recurrence.
Discuss disposition of distressed slabs at pre-construction meetings.
Four commonly encountered early distress types: plastic shrinkage cracking, edge slump, joint spalling, full-depth cracking.
sections.applicability: Applies as the framing introduction whenever early-age distress is observed in a concrete pavement during or shortly after construction.

sections.title: Plastic Shrinkage Cracking
sections.summary: Describes plastic shrinkage cracking as surface cracking from high surface evaporation rates, typically shallow (25-75 mm / 1-3 in.) closely spaced parallel cracks. Covers coring to determine depth, and repair by low-viscosity epoxy or high molecular weight methacrylate injection, with gravity-fed epoxy discouraged and deep cracking requiring slab replacement.
sections.body: Plastic shrinkage cracking is surface cracking that may develop if the rate of evaporation at the surface is high. It typically manifests as shallow, 25 to 75 mm (1 to 3 in.) deep, closely spaced parallel cracks. In some cases the cracking may extend deeper than 75 mm (3 in.), but it is unusual for the cracks to be full depth. It is recommended to take 100-mm (4 in.)-diameter cores over a few cracks to determine the depth of cracking before selecting a repair method. Repair plastic shrinkage cracking by injecting low-viscosity epoxy or high molecular weight methacrylate into each crack after the concrete has hardened, following the epoxy manufacturer's injection procedures. The gravity-fed epoxy technique is not recommended because crack penetration with that method is not fully effective. Cracking deeper than 75 mm (3 in.), or cracking that is extensive, requires slab removal and replacement per paragraph 11-5 (Full-Depth Cracking).
key_points: Plastic shrinkage cracking results from a high rate of surface evaporation.
Typical crack depth is shallow: 25 to 75 mm (1 to 3 in.), closely spaced and parallel.
Take 100-mm (4 in.)-diameter cores over a few cracks to determine actual crack depth.
Repair by injecting low-viscosity epoxy or high molecular weight methacrylate after the concrete has hardened, per manufacturer's procedures.
Gravity-fed epoxy injection is not recommended; it does not achieve full crack penetration.
Cracking deeper than 75 mm (3 in.) or extensive cracking requires slab removal and replacement (paragraph 11-5).
sections.applicability: Applies when shallow, closely spaced parallel surface cracking consistent with high evaporation rate is observed on freshly placed concrete pavement.

sections.title: Edge Slump
sections.summary: Describes edge slump as the tendency of an unsupported slipform-paved edge to slump down as the paver pulls forward, with depression extending inward. Excessive edge slump requires adjusting the mixture, equipment, or operation; it is a serious defect because it can pond water and affect joint performance.
sections.body: When a slipform paver pulls forward, there is a tendency for the unsupported edge to slump down at the edge, with the depression extending inwards on the slab. If excessive edge slump occurs, the concrete mixture, the paving equipment, or the paving operation must be adjusted. Edge slump is a serious defect because it creates an area for ponding of water and can affect joint performance.
key_points: Edge slump occurs as the unsupported slab edge sags when a slipform paver pulls forward.
Depression from edge slump extends inward on the slab.
Excessive edge slump requires adjustment of concrete mixture, paving equipment, or paving operation.
Edge slump is a serious defect: it ponds water and can affect joint performance.
sections.applicability: Applies to slipform-paved concrete pavements exhibiting sagging or depression along the unsupported paving edge.

sections.title: Plastic Repair
sections.summary: Covers plastic (pre-initial-set) repair of edge slump, listing nine items to consider: forming the edge, avoiding plain mortar addition, vibrating repair material into existing concrete, not repairing after curing compound application, the ineffectiveness of vibration once initial set occurs, spalling risk from mortar/hardened-concrete addition, finishing to match surrounding concrete, matching texture/cure, and treating plastic repairs as an exception rather than routine.
sections.body: If edge slump is detected before initial set of the concrete, a plastic repair can be attempted. The repair of edge slump must be carried out correctly to ensure durability of the repaired area. Important items to consider are: the edge must be formed along the repair area; if additional material must be added to repair the edge slump, that material must contain a mixture of aggregate particles, and plain mortar addition is not allowed; the repair area material must be vibrated into the existing material; repair should not be attempted after curing compound has been applied, because the repair area concrete can become contaminated with the curing compound; if initial set has occurred, vibration is ineffective and it is too late to make a plastic edge slump repair; use of plain mortar or addition of material to hardened concrete may lead to spalling; after vibrating the repaired concrete, screed and finish it as uniformly as possible with the surrounding concrete; texture and cure the repaired area using the same processes as the surrounding concrete; and plastic repairs should be the exception, not a routine occurrence. If excessive edge slump is occurring repeatedly, paving should be stopped until the underlying problem is corrected.
key_points: Plastic repair is only viable before initial set of the concrete.
Form the edge along the repair area.
Added material must contain aggregate particles; plain mortar addition is not allowed.
Vibrate the repair material into the existing material.
Do not attempt repair after curing compound has been applied (contamination risk).
After initial set, vibration is ineffective and plastic repair is no longer possible.
Plain mortar or material added to hardened concrete may lead to spalling.
Screed and finish the repaired area uniformly with surrounding concrete, then match texture and curing.
Plastic repairs should be the exception; stop paving if excessive edge slump recurs.
sections.applicability: Applies when edge slump is detected on fresh concrete that has not yet reached initial set, allowing an in-place plastic repair rather than removal.

sections.title: Hardened Pavement
sections.summary: Covers repair options for edge slump once concrete has hardened and a plastic repair could not be performed in a timely manner: either sawing the slumped edge and performing a partial-depth repair at the surface depression, or removing and replacing the slab exhibiting excessive edge slump.
sections.body: If edge slump repair cannot be done in a timely manner (i.e., before initial set), it may be necessary to allow the affected slab panels to harden and repair the defect afterward, either by sawing the slumped edge and performing a partial-depth repair at the surface depression, or by removing and replacing the slab panel that has excessive edge slump.
key_points: Applies when plastic repair cannot be performed in time and the affected panels are allowed to harden.
Option 1: saw the slumped edge and perform a partial-depth repair at the surface depression.
Option 2: remove and replace the slab panel with excessive edge slump.
sections.applicability: Applies when edge slump is discovered after the concrete has already hardened, precluding a plastic repair.

sections.title: Joint Spalling
sections.summary: Covers joint spalling and excessive joint raveling arising from the joint sawing operation, typically due to early sawing, wrong blade type, or poor sawing equipment operation. Minor/localized spalling is repaired with a partial-depth technique using the paving concrete mixture; severe/excessive spalling warrants slab replacement.
sections.body: Joint spalling or excessive joint raveling may develop as a result of the joint sawing operation, typically due to early joint sawing, use of the wrong blade type, or poor operation of the sawing equipment. Minor or localized joint spalling is typically repaired using a partial-depth repair technique with the concrete mixture used for paving. If the spalling is severe and excessive in length, replacement of the affected slab should be considered.
key_points: Joint spalling/raveling typically results from early sawing, wrong blade type, or poor sawing equipment operation.
Minor or localized joint spalling: repair with a partial-depth repair technique using the paving concrete mixture.
Severe or excessive-length spalling: consider replacing the affected slab.
sections.applicability: Applies when spalling or raveling is observed along a sawed joint in a concrete pavement.

sections.title: Full-Depth Cracking
sections.summary: Covers localized full-depth cracking, listing seven possible causes (late/insufficient transverse joint sawing, misaligned dowel bars, excessive curling/warping, rapid surface cooling, early-age construction loading, excessive drying shrinkage, excessive base frictional restraint). Cracking within 30 days usually indicates poor construction practice or design. Presents six repair-decision items (a-f) for critical vs. non-critical pavement areas, plus detailed slab removal/replacement procedures.
sections.body: Localized full-depth cracking may result from late transverse joint sawing or insufficient depth of sawing, misaligned dowel bars, excessive curling or warping, rapid surface cooling, early-age loading by construction equipment, excessive drying shrinkage, or excessive base frictional restraint. Full-depth cracking that appears within 30 days is usually the result of poor construction practices, poor design, or both. Important items to consider for repair of full-depth cracking are as follows. Replace panels in critical pavement areas (those subject to aircraft landing gear loading) where full-depth cracking extends the full width or length of the slab panel. Full-depth cracking in non-critical pavement areas (most exterior lanes of a runway or taxiway) may be left in place at the option of the owner, with the crack routed and sealed. Treat full-depth cracking in critical pavement areas that extends less than one-third the width or length of the slab as full-width cracking. Repair full-depth corner cracking in critical pavement areas by full panel replacement. Avoid using partial panel replacement in critical pavement areas on new pavement. Follow proper procedures for slab removal and replacement, which must include the following: remove slabs without damaging adjacent sound slabs or the base, using double saw cutting along the slab perimeter, no heavy impact loading to break the slab into small pieces, and sawcutting the panel into smaller segments to lift out; inspect the base for damage and correct it before concrete placement; restore load transfer along all joints with dowel bars using the drill-and-epoxy grouting technique; use approved concrete mixtures for hand placement operations; use vibration to consolidate the concrete; and use proper techniques to finish, texture, and cure the replacement slab.
key_points: Possible causes: late/insufficient transverse joint sawing, misaligned dowel bars, excessive curling/warping, rapid surface cooling, early-age construction equipment loading, excessive drying shrinkage, excessive base frictional restraint.
Cracking appearing within 30 days usually indicates poor construction practice, poor design, or both.
Critical pavement areas (aircraft landing gear loading) with full-width/length cracking: replace the panel.
Non-critical areas (most exterior runway/taxiway lanes): crack may be left in place at owner's option, routed and sealed.
Cracking in critical areas extending less than one-third the slab width/length: treat as full-width cracking.
Full-depth corner cracking in critical areas: repair by full panel replacement; avoid partial panel replacement on new pavement.
Slab removal must avoid damaging adjacent slabs/base: double saw cutting, no heavy impact loading, sawcut into segments and lift out.
Inspect and correct base damage before placing replacement concrete.
Restore load transfer at all joints using dowel bars installed by drill-and-epoxy grouting.
Use approved mixtures for hand placement, vibrate to consolidate, and finish/texture/cure to match surrounding pavement.
sections.applicability: Applies when full-depth cracking is observed in concrete pavement panels, governing both the repair-vs-replace decision and the procedures for slab removal and replacement.
